Meanwhile, a database cache keeps frequently requested results in fast memory, so applications avoid repeating costly queries against slower storage; the cache therefore reduces latency, lowers load on the primary server, and lets systems serve many more users each second.

However, speed has a price, because stored copies can drift away from the truth. Teams therefore choose expiry times, invalidate entries after writes, and monitor hit rates carefully; a cache with poor eviction rules wastes memory, while a well tuned cache quietly absorbs enormous traffic without surprising anyone, even during sudden big holiday shopping spikes.

Along with growth, a busy log of data must go through lots of slow disk work; but a fast mapping in main RAM can sit by to catch calls and cut wait. Tuning of this stash is tricky, as old facts can fool us, so a solid plan for purging old rows is vital.

Finally, measure results, keep each cache small and relevant, test failures early, and stay reliable when the work is done.
